Topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Mathematical Secret

Target audience: Middle to High school students

Section: section_1 — The Binary Language (Prerequisite)

Lecture lines:
Binary uses only zero and one digits.
Each position represents a power of two.
Light switches visualize binary states perfectly.

Planned animations:
Create a sequence of zeros and ones on screen.
Highlight a single bit, color it #FFD700 (Gold).
Flash the bit to signify its importance.

Section: section_2 — The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle

Lecture lines:
Move disks from start to end peg.
Never place larger disks on smaller ones.
Move one disk at a time only.

Planned animations:
Display three pegs with a stack of disks.
Highlight the smallest disk, color it #FF4500 (OrangeRed).
Animate the disk moving from peg A to C.

Section: section_3 — Mapping Moves to Binary

Lecture lines:
Hanoi moves match the binary sequence.
Three disks require seven total moves.
Binary count zero-zero-one is move one.
Binary count one-one-one is move seven.
The sequence maps binary to disk movement.

Planned animations:
Show a disk moving and a binary digit changing.
Use a connecting line, color #00CED1 (DarkTurquoise).
Synchronize the disk shift with the digit flip.

Section: section_4 — The Algorithmic Logic

Lecture lines:
Small disks move every other turn.
Middle disks move every four turns.
Large disks move every eight turns.
Smallest disk moves at every odd step.
Movement follows a perfect recursive pattern.

Planned animations:
Present the recursive formula: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1.
Highlight the '2' and '+1' in #32CD32 (LimeGreen).
Animate the recursive calls branching out like trees.

Section: section_5 — Summary and Real-world Application

Lecture lines:
Recursion is the engine of movement.
Binary is the DNA of logic.
Computer chips process data like Hanoi.

Planned animations:
Display a computer chip image as.
Superimpose the disk tower logic onto the chip.
Fade in 'Efficiency' label in #FFFFFF (White).
